title: AC Sources & Circuits

notes.heading: 1. Sinusoidal RMS, Half-Cycle Average, Form Factor & Crest Factor
notes.proseLatex: For a pure sine wave $v(t) = V_m\sin(\omega t + \phi)$ ($\omega = 2\pi f$), effective heating value is $V_{\text{rms}} = \frac{V_m}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707\,V_m$ and half-cycle rectified average is $V_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2V_m}{\pi} \approx 0.637\,V_m$ (full-cycle average is $0$). Form factor is $K_f = \frac{V_{\text{rms}}}{V_{\text{avg}}} = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}} \approx 1.11$ and peak/crest factor is $K_p = \frac{V_m}{V_{\text{rms}}} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$ (for a symmetric square wave, $K_f = K_p = 1$; for a half-wave rectified sine, $V_{\text{rms}} = V_m/2$ and $V_{\text{avg}} = V_m/\pi$!).

keyFormulas.label: Sine, Half-Wave & Square-Wave RMS / Form Factor
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Recall exact RMS, average, form factor, and peak factor of standard waveforms.

notes.heading: 2. Series RLC Impedance, Resonance, Q-Factor & Bandwidth
notes.proseLatex: Series RLC impedance is $Z = R + j(X_L - X_C)$ where $X_L = \omega L$ (current LAGS voltage by $90^\circ$ in pure $L$) and $X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}$ (current LEADS voltage by $90^\circ$ in pure $C$), with $|Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$. At series resonance ($X_L = X_C \implies f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$), impedance hits its MINIMUM $|Z|_{\min} = R$, current hits its MAXIMUM $V/R$ at UNITY power factor ($\cos\phi = 1$), and reactive voltages magnify to $Q V$ where quality factor $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \frac{f_0}{\text{BW}}$!

keyFormulas.label: Series RLC Impedance, Resonant Frequency & Q-Factor
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Compute resonant frequency, half-power bandwidth, Q-factor, and voltage magnification.

examples.problemLatex: A series RLC circuit with $R = 10\,\Omega,\; L = 0.1\text{ H},\; C = 10\,\mu\text{F}$ is excited at resonance. Find $\omega_0$, quality factor $Q$, and bandwidth in $\text{rad/s}$.

notes.heading: 3. Active, Reactive & Apparent Power Triangle
notes.proseLatex: Using RMS magnitudes $V, I$ and impedance phase $\phi$: Active (real) power $P = VI\cos\phi = I^2 R$ ($\text{W}$), Reactive power $Q = VI\sin\phi = I^2(X_L - X_C)$ ($\text{VAR}$), and Apparent power $S = VI = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2}$ ($\text{VA}$), with power factor $\cos\phi = R/|Z| = P/S$ (pure $L$ or pure $C$ consumes ZERO average real power, $\cos\phi = 0$!). In balanced $3$-phase circuits: Star ($\text{Y}$) has $V_L = \sqrt{3}V_{\text{ph}},\; I_L = I_{\text{ph}}$; Delta ($\Delta$) has $V_L = V_{\text{ph}},\; I_L = \sqrt{3}I_{\text{ph}}$; and BOTH obey $P_{3\phi} = \sqrt{3}V_L I_L\cos\phi$.

keyFormulas.label: AC Power Triangle & Balanced 3-Phase Power
keyFormulas.latex: $P = VI\cos\phi,\quad Q = VI\sin\phi,\quad S = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2},\quad P_{3\phi} = \sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L\cos\phi$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Calculate real/reactive/apparent power, power factor, and 3-phase Y/Delta line relations.

wbjeebTraps: Series vs Parallel resonance flip: SERIES resonance gives MINIMUM $|Z| = R$ and MAXIMUM current; PARALLEL (tank) resonance gives MAXIMUM $|Z|$ (rejector circuit) and MINIMUM line current!
Never add AC series branch voltages algebraically: $V_S = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}$, so at resonance $V_L = V_C = QV_S$ can easily exceed supply voltage $V_S$!
Remember bandwidth units: $\Delta\omega = R/L$ is in $\text{rad/s}$, whereas $\Delta f = \frac{R}{2\pi L}$ is in $\text{Hz}$!

conceptPrimer.heading: Why AC Needs an RMS — Heat Is the Referee
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: A sinusoidal current is negative for half of every cycle, so its plain average over a full period is ZERO — yet it still lights lamps, because heating goes as $i^2$, which is always positive. The root-mean-square value is the DC current that would deliver the same heating: square it, average it, take the square root — hence $I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{i_m}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707\, i_m$ for a sine. Unless a question states otherwise, every AC meter reading and every power formula speaks RMS (mains '220 V' is an RMS value; its peak is $220\sqrt{2} \approx 311\text{ V}$). The mean value is quoted over a HALF cycle for the same full-cycle-cancellation reason: $\frac{2 i_m}{\pi} \approx 0.637\, i_m$.

conceptPrimer.heading: L and C Fight the Change — One Lags, One Leads
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: An inductor opposes any change in current (its back-emf follows Lenz's law), so in a pure inductor the current LAGS the voltage by $90^{\circ}$, and the opposition it offers is $X_L = \omega L$, which GROWS with frequency. A capacitor opposes any change in voltage (the current must charge it first), so the current LEADS by $90^{\circ}$, and its opposition $X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}$ SHRINKS as frequency rises. Because those two phase shifts point in opposite directions, $X_L$ and $X_C$ partially cancel in a series circuit: $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$. This is also why series branch voltages must never be added arithmetically — they are out of phase, and only their phasor (Pythagorean) sum equals the source voltage.

conceptPrimer.heading: Resonance and the Power Factor — AC Behaves Like DC
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: At $\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$ the two reactances match ($X_L = X_C$) and cancel completely: impedance collapses to its minimum $Z = R$, current peaks, and the power factor hits unity — for that one frequency the circuit behaves like a pure resistor. The price of the cancellation is voltage magnification: at resonance $V_L = V_C = Q V_S$, where $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R}$ measures how sharply the circuit selects its frequency (higher $Q$, taller and narrower peak). Away from resonance, real power still flows only through the resistance: $P = V I \cos\phi$. A pure $L$ or $C$ draws 'wattless' current ($\cos\phi = 0$) — it borrows energy and hands it all back, net zero over a cycle.

memoryHooks: The four sine numbers: RMS $= 0.707\,V_m$, half-cycle average $= 0.637\,V_m$, form factor $= 1.11$, peak factor $= 1.414$.
ELI the ICE man: in L (ELI), voltage E leads current I; in C (ICE), current I leads voltage E.
$X_L = \omega L$ climbs with frequency; $X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}$ dives — they cross at resonance.
Series resonance trio: $Z$ minimum $= R$, current maximum, power factor $= 1$.
$\omega = 2\pi f$ — convert to angular form BEFORE computing any reactance.
Real power lives in $R$ only: $P = VI\cos\phi = I^2 R$, with $\cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z}$.
commonMistakes: Mixing peak and RMS: inserting $V_m$ or $i_m$ into $P = VI\cos\phi$ — power formulas accept RMS values only.
Adding $X_L$ and $X_C$ as if both were positive: the net reactance is $X_L - X_C$, and its SIGN decides whether the circuit is net-inductive (current lags) or net-capacitive (current leads).
Reporting 'average value of AC is zero' and then refusing to compute the half-cycle mean when a question explicitly asks for the average (mean) value.
Treating an ideal inductor or capacitor as a power consumer — each returns every joule it borrows; the average power over a cycle is zero and only $R$ dissipates.
Quoting $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R}$ while forgetting the same $R$ sits in the equivalent form $Q = \frac{1}{\omega_0 C R}$ — dropping $R$ (or using $L$ and $C$ inconsistently) inflates the factor.
examChecklist: Open every AC question by fixing the vocabulary: $v = V_m \sin \omega t$, $\omega = 2\pi f$, $T = \frac{1}{f}$.
Know which factor is which: form factor $= \frac{\text{RMS}}{\text{average}} = 1.11$, peak (crest) factor $= \frac{V_m}{V_{\text{rms}}} = 1.414$ for a sine.
For any series RLC: sketch the impedance triangle ($R$, $X_L - X_C$, hypotenuse $Z$) before computing $\phi$ or the power factor.
State the resonance set together: $f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$, $Z_{\min} = R$, $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{\omega_0 C R}$.
Power questions: $P = VI\cos\phi$ with RMS magnitudes, where $\phi$ is the angle between V and I phasors.
Quote units deliberately: reactances in $\Omega$ after the $\omega$ conversion; bandwidth flagged as rad/s ($\Delta\omega = \frac{R}{L}$) or Hz ($\Delta f = \frac{R}{2\pi L}$).
Reject any series-RLC answer with $Z < R$ — outside resonance $Z$ can never dip below $R$.
